questions.stem: The National Insurance Commission (NAICOM) was established by:

opts.x: The National Insurance Commission Act 1997 (Decree No. 1 of 1997).
The Chartered Insurance Institute of Nigeria Act 1993.

questions.answer: (C) The National Insurance Commission Act 1997 (Decree No. 1 of 1997).

why.h: Why (C) is Correct

NAICOM was established by the NAICOM Act 1997 (originally enacted as Decree No. 1 of 1997), which constituted it as an independent statutory body with its own corporate structure, leadership, and mandate. The NAICOM Act remains in force alongside NIIRA 2025. NAICOM predates both the Insurance Act 2003 and NIIRA 2025 by several years.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) The Insurance Act 2003 provided the regulatory framework governing insurers but did not establish NAICOM — NAICOM already existed and enforced the Act.

(B) NIIRA 2025 significantly expanded NAICOM’s powers but did not create it; NAICOM has operated continuously since 1997.

(D) The CIIN Act 1993 established the Chartered Insurance Institute of Nigeria as the professional qualification body, not the regulatory authority.

questions.stem: Under NIIRA 2025, the minimum capital requirement for a life insurance company is:

why.h: Why (C) is Correct

NIIRA 2025 Part II sets the minimum paid-up capital for a life-only insurance licence at ₦10 billion. This is a fivefold increase from the pre-NIIRA 2025 minimum of ₦2 billion, designed to ensure life insurers have sufficient capital to meet the increased claims obligations of a growing policy portfolio and the demands of the new Risk-Based Capital framework.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) ₦2bn was the minimum under the repealed Insurance Act 2003 — it no longer applies.

(B) ₦8bn does not correspond to any NIIRA 2025 minimum capital threshold.

(D) ₦15bn is the minimum for general (non-life) insurance, not life insurance. Life and general licences have different thresholds (life ₦10bn, non-life ₦15bn).

questions.stem: Which ONE of the following was NOT repealed by NIIRA 2025?

opts.x: Nigeria Reinsurance Corporation Act, Cap. N131

questions.answer: (C) National Insurance Commission Act 1997 — this was NOT repealed.

why.h: Why (C) is Correct

The NAICOM Act 1997 was expressly preserved by NIIRA 2025. It continues to provide NAICOM’s institutional framework and founding powers. NIIRA 2025 supplemented and expanded NAICOM’s mandate without replacing its founding statute. This is the only one of the four options that survives.
Why the Others Were Repealed

(A) The Insurance Act, Cap I17 (LFN 2004) was expressly repealed and replaced in its entirety by NIIRA 2025 — this was the principal statute being reformed.

(B) The Marine Insurance Act, Cap M2 was swept up in NIIRA 2025’s comprehensive consolidation of insurance legislation.

(D) The Nigeria Reinsurance Corporation Act, Cap N131 was also repealed. The NRC is now regulated under NIIRA 2025’s reinsurance provisions.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a statutory requirement for an individual to be licensed as an insurance agent under s.37(2) of NIIRA 2025?

opts.x: A university degree in business or economics.
A certificate of proficiency issued by the Chartered Insurance Institute of Nigeria (CIIN).
Five years’ experience as a licensed insurance broker.

questions.answer: (B) A certificate of proficiency issued by the Chartered Insurance Institute of Nigeria (CIIN).

why.h: Why (B) is Correct

Section 37(2) of NIIRA 2025 provides that a person shall not be licensed as an insurance agent unless he holds a certificate of proficiency issued by the CIIN. The same subsection also requires at least 10 years’ experience or length of service in an underwriting firm, no conviction for an offence involving dishonesty or fraud, and no bankruptcy in the preceding five years. For a corporate agent, at least one principal officer must hold the certificate. The licence is renewable after three years (s.37(8)).
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) The Act sets no degree requirement.

(C) FCIIN is the CIIN’s highest qualification; the Act asks only for a certificate of proficiency.

(D) The experience the Act requires is at least 10 years in an underwriting firm, not five years as a broker; brokers are licensed separately under s.39.

questions.stem: The final deadline for all insurers and reinsurers to comply with NIIRA 2025’s recapitalisation requirements is:

why.h: Why (D) is Correct

The NAICOM Recapitalisation Implementation Directive (2025) sets 30 July 2026 as the final deadline for all licensed insurers and reinsurers to achieve full compliance with NIIRA 2025’s minimum capital thresholds. This allows approximately 12 months from the Act’s commencement (August 2025) for the final compliance phase.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) 30 September 2025 was the deadline for insurers to submit their recapitalisation plans and financial statements to NAICOM, not the final compliance deadline.

(B) 31 December 2025 is not a NIIRA 2025 recapitalisation deadline.

(C) 30 June 2026 is an interim milestone deadline under the recapitalisation programme, not the final deadline.

questions.stem: Describe the Risk-Based Capital (RBC) framework introduced by NIIRA 2025. Explain how RBC differs from the flat Minimum Capital Requirement (MCR), identify the categories of risk that RBC takes into account, and explain why NAICOM has adopted a dual capital standard (higher of MCR and RBC applies) rather than a simple flat minimum.

model.h: RBC vs Minimum Capital Requirement (MCR)

The Minimum Capital Requirement (MCR) is a flat absolute floor: every licenced life insurer must hold a minimum of ₦10 billion in paid-up capital regardless of the risks it runs. A small insurer writing ₦500m in low-risk term assurance and a large composite writing ₦50bn in complex annuities and unit-linked products both face the same nominal floor.

Risk-Based Capital (RBC) is fundamentally different: the capital requirement is calculated from the insurer’s actual risk profile. An insurer with a large, concentrated investment portfolio, volatile mortality experience, and heavy reinsurer counterparty exposure is required to hold more capital than one with a stable, diversified, low-risk book. RBC calibrates capital to risk.
Categories of Risk in the NIIRA 2025 RBC Framework

The RBC formula under NIIRA 2025 aggregates five risk categories:

1. Insurance risk: the risk that mortality, morbidity, or lapse experience is materially worse than priced assumptions.
2. Market risk: the risk that investment portfolio values fall due to interest rate movements, equity market declines, or real estate devaluation.
3. Credit risk: the risk of default by reinsurers (on recoveries), brokers (on premiums held), and other counterparties.
4. Operational risk: the risk of loss from failed processes, system failures, fraud, or regulatory sanctions.
5. Liquidity risk: the risk of being unable to meet cash claims obligations as they fall due, even if the insurer is technically solvent.
Why NAICOM Adopted a Dual Capital Standard

NAICOM retained the MCR as an absolute minimum alongside the RBC formula because:

1. Data and actuarial capacity: Many Nigerian insurers do not yet have the actuarial sophistication and data infrastructure to produce reliable RBC calculations. An insurer with poor data might calculate an artificially low RBC requirement, understating its true capital need. The MCR prevents this.

2. Market stability: During the transition to RBC, the MCR provides a stable compliance anchor. If an insurer’s RBC calculation in the first year of implementation produces an anomalous result (due to data errors or model misspecification), the MCR ensures a meaningful minimum is maintained.

3. Prudential buffer: For very small insurers with simple risk profiles, the RBC formula might produce a capital requirement below ₦10bn. The MCR ensures that even simple, low-risk books are backed by substantive capital.

Result: An insurer must hold the higher of MCR and its calculated RBC requirement at all times.

questions.stem:
XYZ Life Insurance Company Limited has a current capital base of ₦6 billion. It is a life-only insurer in operation since 2010.
(a) Calculate the capital shortfall XYZ Life must address under NIIRA 2025.
(b) Describe the compliance process — key dates and documentation requirements — for the recapitalisation programme.
(c) Identify and evaluate three strategic options available to XYZ Life to achieve compliance by 30 July 2026, noting the advantages and risks of each.

model.h: Part (a) — Capital Shortfall Calculation

NIIRA 2025 minimum capital for life insurance: ₦10,000,000,000.
XYZ Life current capital: ₦6,000,000,000.
Capital shortfall: ₦10,000,000,000 − ₦6,000,000,000 = ₦4,000,000,000 (Four Billion Naira).
Part (b) — Compliance Process and Key Dates

Step 1 — Recapitalisation Plan Submission: XYZ Life must submit a Board-approved Recapitalisation Plan to NAICOM by 30 September 2025. The plan must include: the chosen route to compliance; a detailed timeline; the source of capital; supporting documents (term sheets, MoUs with investors, draft merger agreement if applicable); Board resolution; and CFO certification that the plan is achievable.

Step 2 — Interim Milestones: The NAICOM Recapitalisation Directive sets phased milestones:
• Milestone 1 (12 months from commencement, August 2026 equivalent): 25% of gap closed — capital reaches ₦7bn.
• Milestone 2 (24 months): 50% closed — capital reaches ₦8bn.
• Final deadline (30 July 2026 for the accelerated single-year track): 100% compliance at ₦10bn.

Documentation at each milestone: quarterly capital adequacy return to NAICOM; auditor’s confirmation letter; Board resolution confirming ongoing compliance.
Part (c) — Three Strategic Options

Option 1 — Fresh Equity Capital Injection:
Structure: Issue new shares to existing or new investors to raise ₦4bn.
Advantage: XYZ Life retains its brand, management team, and independence. If existing shareholders are supportive and have the financial capacity, this is the simplest structural option.
Risk: Finding investors willing to commit ₦4bn requires a credible business case and may result in significant dilution of existing shareholders. Investor due diligence and regulatory approval will take several months.

Option 2 — Rights Issue:
Structure: Offer new shares to existing shareholders at a preferential price, entitling them to subscribe proportionately.
Advantage: Retains existing shareholder ownership structure; preserves goodwill and institutional continuity.
Risk: Existing shareholders must have the capacity and willingness to subscribe. If the rights issue is not fully taken up, XYZ Life may still face a shortfall and must find alternative investors for the unsubscribed portion within the deadline.

Option 3 — Merger or Acquisition:
Structure: Merge with another life insurer to create a combined entity with aggregate capital exceeding ₦10bn.
Advantage: Merger can simultaneously address capital, scale, distribution, and talent — potentially creating a stronger market competitor than either entity alone.
Risk: NAICOM must approve the merger before execution; due diligence, court sanction, and NAICOM approval could take 12–18 months, leaving the timeline extremely tight. Cultural and operational integration of two businesses is a significant management challenge post-merger.
(a) Nigerian Insurers Association (NIA)

Role: The NIA is the trade association for all licensed insurance companies in Nigeria. It is a voluntary membership organisation representing the collective commercial interests of insurers.

Functions: Industry statistics publication (annual market data report); collective advocacy with NAICOM and the legislature on regulatory developments; management of the Motor Third Party Claims Bureau (administering third-party motor claims against uninsured drivers); industry training and capacity-building initiatives; liaison with international bodies (including AfricaRe and the African Insurance Organisation).

Interaction with NAICOM: NAICOM consults the NIA on regulatory proposals (NIIRA 2025 was preceded by NIA consultation). The NIA does not exercise regulatory functions itself. It acts as the industry’s collective voice in a non-adversarial relationship with NAICOM.
(b) Nigerian Council of Registered Insurance Brokers (NCRIB)

Role: The professional and regulatory body for insurance brokers, established under the NCRIB Act 1991.

Functions: Maintaining the register of licensed insurance brokers; setting and enforcing professional standards for the brokerage profession; administering CPD requirements; representing broker interests before NAICOM; liaising with international broker bodies.

Interaction with NAICOM: NAICOM licences insurance brokers under NIIRA 2025; NCRIB assists in setting the professional standards against which licensing assessments are made. There is a complementary relationship — NAICOM holds the regulatory power; NCRIB provides the professional infrastructure.
(c) Chartered Insurance Institute of Nigeria (CIIN)

Role: The professional qualification body for insurance in Nigeria, established under the CIIN Act 1993.

Functions: Setting and examining the qualification pathway (Cert. COP, Certificate, Diploma, Associateship, Fellowship); maintaining the CPD framework for qualified members; professional disciplinary processes; publishing the Nigerian Insurance Journal; conducting insurance education programmes.

Interaction with NAICOM: NIIRA 2025 expressly requires Cert. COP as a prerequisite for all insurance sales staff — creating a statutory link between CIIN’s qualification infrastructure and NAICOM’s licensing regime. CIIN’s examination standards become, in effect, a regulatory tool.
(d) Institute of Loss Adjusters of Nigeria (ILAN)

Role: The professional body for licensed loss adjusters in Nigeria.

Functions: Maintaining the register of qualified loss adjusters; setting professional standards for claims assessment; administering professional discipline; representing the profession before NAICOM.

Interaction with NAICOM: NIIRA 2025 requires loss adjusters to hold ILAN-prescribed qualifications and to maintain professional indemnity insurance. NAICOM issues the loss adjuster licence; ILAN provides the professional standards framework that underpins the licensing requirements.

questions.stem: NIIRA 2025 has been described by Commissioner Omosehin as 'a once-in-a-generation opportunity to reposition the Nigerian insurance industry for sustainable growth and innovation.' Critically assess this claim, examining the key innovations of the Act — particularly the RBC framework, the raised MCRs, Insurtech licensing, and enhanced consumer protection — against the structural challenges that have historically limited Nigeria's insurance penetration to below 0.5% of GDP.

model.h: Essay Framework
Thesis

NIIRA 2025 is the best regulatory foundation the Nigerian insurance industry has ever had. It is a necessary but insufficient condition for the penetration growth Nigeria’s insurance market needs. The characterisation of it as ‘once-in-a-generation’ is justified in scope; its transformation depends on execution.
What NIIRA 2025 Achieves

1. Risk-Based Capital: For the first time, capital requirements are calibrated to actual risk. Well-managed insurers are rewarded with lower proportionate capital requirements; poorly managed ones face higher demands. This creates efficiency incentives.

2. Raised MCRs: The fivefold increase in life insurance minimum capital (₦2bn → ₦10bn) will force consolidation of the weakest players. Fewer, better-capitalised insurers improve the industry’s ability to meet claims — the foundational trust issue.

3. Insurtech licensing: The formal Partnering and Standalone Insurtech tracks create a regulatory pathway for digital distribution. The 220 million Nigerians who cannot be reached by conventional agent distribution can theoretically be reached through mobile-distributed insurance.

4. Enhanced consumer protection: The 60-day claims mandate, the Policyholders’ Protection Fund, the TCF obligation, and the improved complaints redress framework directly address the trust deficit mechanisms.
What NIIRA 2025 Cannot Do

1. Rebuild trust directly: Trust is rebuilt through consistent, excellent claims service over years. Legislation creates incentives and consequences; it cannot change insurer culture overnight.

2. Reduce poverty: Nigeria’s low penetration is partly a function of income levels below which insurance is not affordable. No regulatory reform changes the income distribution.

3. Improve financial literacy: The majority of Nigerians do not understand what insurance is or how it works. Regulation cannot substitute for sustained financial education.

4. Fix the distribution gap alone: Insurtech licensing opens the door; Insurtechs must then build and earn trust in the same markets where conventional insurers have failed for decades.
Conclusion

Commissioner Omosehin’s ‘once-in-a-generation’ characterisation is accurate as an assessment of the legislative opportunity. NIIRA 2025 is the most comprehensive reform Nigeria has had. Whether it fulfils the opportunity depends on: NAICOM’s enforcement energy; insurers’ willingness to genuinely change their claims culture; the industry’s investment in digital distribution; and the government’s commitment to financial literacy and financial inclusion as national policy priorities.

questions.stem: Compulsory insurance has existed in Nigerian law since the 1960s, yet enforcement has historically been weak. Analyse the enforcement mechanisms available under NIIRA 2025 — including the NAICOM-BPP MoU, digital verification systems, and expanded NAICOM enforcement powers — and evaluate whether they are likely to be more effective than prior enforcement attempts. Consider the structural, political, and institutional factors that have historically undermined compulsory insurance compliance in Nigeria.

model.h: Essay Framework
Thesis

Compulsory insurance’s chronic enforcement failure in Nigeria reflects a structural problem: enforcement requires sustained multi-agency coordination, political will to act against well-connected non-compliers, and institutional capacity that NAICOM has historically lacked. NIIRA 2025’s mechanisms are meaningfully stronger than their predecessors on all three dimensions, but the test is execution over time.
Historical Enforcement Failures

Three structural causes of historical failure:

1. Weak institutional capacity: Early NAICOM had insufficient staff and budget to inspect more than a fraction of the insured population. Motor TPMI enforcement required cooperation with VIO and police, which was inconsistent and corruption-prone.

2. Fictitious certificate market: A thriving market in fake motor insurance certificates made enforcement technically difficult — the VIO officer on the road could not verify authenticity.

3. Political economy: Enforcing group life compliance against major employers or government agencies required political courage that was often absent. State governments were chronically non-compliant on civil servant group life.
NIIRA 2025 Enforcement Improvements

1. Digital certificate verification: NAICOM’s online portal enables instant verification of genuine insurance certificates from a mobile device. This directly attacks the fictitious certificate market — a VIO officer with a smartphone can verify in seconds whether a certificate is real.

2. NAICOM-BPP MoU: Companies seeking government contracts through the Bureau of Public Procurement must now demonstrate compulsory insurance compliance. This creates a powerful non-regulatory lever — the loss of government business is a severe commercial consequence.

3. CAC integration: Companies renewing CAC registration may be required to provide evidence of compulsory insurance. This embeds compliance into the annual corporate administration cycle rather than making it a standalone regulatory exercise.

4. Expanded NAICOM powers: Higher fines, criminal liability for directors of non-compliant organisations, and the power to name non-compliers publicly.

5. PenCom coordination: The joint PenCom-NAICOM framework for group life enforcement creates dual-agency pressure on non-compliant employers.
Remaining Risks

1. Informal sector: Most Nigerians are employed informally. Neither the BPP MoU nor CAC integration reaches self-employed individuals, agricultural workers, or cooperative enterprises.

2. Enforcement capacity: NAICOM’s inspection team must grow to match the ambition of its enforcement mandate.

3. Political will: Enforcement against state governments and major employers has always been politically sensitive. NIIRA 2025 does not change the political environment, only the legal tools.
Conclusion

NIIRA 2025’s enforcement innovations are genuinely new and genuinely better. The digital verification and BPP integration in particular address structural gaps that made prior enforcement ineffective. The framework is ready; the question is whether NAICOM will use it with the sustained consistency that would allow Nigeria’s compulsory insurance framework to actually function as intended.
